summary: A Harvard Medical School news article (December 8, 2017) reports a mouse study published in Nature Communications showing that social recognition is regulated by oxytocin-sensitive neurons in the dentate gyrus-CA3 (DG-CA3) circuit of the hippocampus. When oxytocin is present, this circuit, which normally separates similar object memories, also regulates social recognition; the signals are relayed via the posterior hippocampus to the nucleus accumbens. The researchers suggest that disruptions in this circuit may relate to autism-spectrum disorders and to PTSD-like overgeneralization of fear.
one_line: Harvard Medical School study in mice finds oxytocin switches a hippocampal memory-separation circuit to regulate social recognition.
key_facts: The study was described December 8, 2017 in Nature Communications and conducted in mice by regenerative neuroscientists at Harvard Medical School, the Harvard Stem Cell Institute and Massachusetts General Hospital.
Social recognition is regulated by a lattice of oxytocin-sensitive neurons in a part of the hippocampus, a seahorse-shaped structure responsible for memory formation.
Computation of social stimuli takes place in the dentate gyrus-CA3 (DG-CA3) circuit, a subunit of the hippocampus thought to file similar memories in distinct folders.
In the absence of oxytocin, the DG-CA3 circuit regulates object recognition; oxytocin acts as a critical catalyst that switches the circuit's functional mode.
Tara Raam, a graduate student in neuroscience at Harvard University, was the study's first author.

Amar Sahay, a Harvard Medical School associate professor, was the senior investigator; he is at the Center for Regenerative Medicine and the Department of Psychiatry at Massachusetts General Hospital.
When oxytocin receptors were deleted in the DG-CA3 circuit, mice could still tell old from new objects but could no longer distinguish familiar mice from unknown mice in social situations.
Optogenetics revealed a neural pathway from DG-CA3 to the posterior hippocampus, then to the nucleus accumbens in the forebrain, which relays social signals.
Sahay said of the mechanism: "Nature is thrifty, it's parsimonious... It repurposes existing ones."

The researchers suggest that disruptions in hippocampal activity may underlie social behavior anomalies in autism-spectrum disorders and other neurodevelopmental, psychiatric and neurologic conditions.
Sahay gave an example of a soldier with PTSD who perceives a benign object resembling an improvised explosive device as a threat, describing it as an overgeneralization of fear.
Oxytocin is known for its role in bonding, empathy and sexual pleasure.

Funding came from NIH BRAINS award 1-R01MH104175, NIH-NIA 1R01AG048908-01, NIH-NIMH 1R01MH111729-01, the Ellison Medical Foundation, the Whitehall Foundation, Inscopix DECODE, NARSAD, the Blue Guitar Fund and the Harvard Neuro Discovery Center.
Co-investigators included Kathleen McAvoy, Antoine Besnard and Alexa Veenema.
